claims.text: Laser cladding WC particles onto an HEA surface will create a reinforced composite coating.
The WC laser-clad coating will reduce coefficient of friction relative to untreated HEA across a broad temperature range.
The WC laser-clad coating will reduce wear rate relative to untreated HEA across a broad temperature range.
The initial self-lubricating HEA components exhibit moderate friction and wear under standard operating conditions.
The treatment will remain effective from ambient temperature to elevated temperatures at which the coating remains thermally stable.
The treatment will remain effective under typical mechanical loading conditions.
Laser cladding will produce a well-dispersed network of WC particles embedded in the HEA matrix.
The WC-containing composite layer will increase surface hardness.
The WC-containing composite layer will distribute contact stresses.
Increased hardness and WC barrier phases will reduce local plastic deformation during sliding.
The composite structure will minimize adhesive wear.
The composite structure will reduce shear at sliding contact interfaces.
Reduced plastic deformation, adhesive wear, and interfacial shear will lower friction and wear.
Laser cladding will provide strong metallurgical bonding that sustains coating performance at high temperatures.
The coating may reduce coefficient of friction by 20% to 40% relative to untreated HEA.
The coating may reduce wear rate by 30% to 50% relative to untreated HEA.
The expected benefits depend on formation of a uniformly bonded composite layer without significant defects.
Extreme thermal cycling, excessive loads, or degraded coating adhesion may eliminate the tribological improvements.
Prior literature suggests that WC reinforcement deposited by laser cladding improves tribological performance.
The proposed comparison uses untreated HEA samples as controls and tests both groups at room temperature, 200°C, and 400°C under identical loads.
